name: The great swap: two directions across the ocean
scope: The two-way flood of foods unleashed by Columbus's 1492 landing (the Columbian Exchange), each rung a concrete crop-and-direction fact. T1: name the source — the potato, tomato, chili, chocolate, and corn (maize) ALL crossed the ocean FROM the Americas to the rest of the world (answer: the Americas / New World). T2: going the other way, Europeans unloaded farm animals the Americas had never had for meat and milk — cattle and pigs (answer: the meat-and-milk animals Europeans introduced = cattle/pigs). T3: the Old World also sent plant crops — the grain Europeans needed to bake their familiar bread in the New World was wheat (answer: the Old World grain planted in the Americas = wheat). T4: New World crops caused population booms far from home — the sweet potato and maize let China's population nearly triple (answer: the American crop that fed Qing China's surge = the sweet potato). T5: the same crops rewrote Africa — cassava from South America became a top staple across the continent (answer: the American root crop Africa adopted as a staple = cassava). Dinner-test: T4/T5, that the ocean-crossing crops fed billions on the far side of the world.
source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbian_exchange; warwick.ac.uk food-history PDF 'New World Foods and Old World Demography'; jameshancockcrophistories.wordpress.com (China & the Columbian Exchange); hungyichen.com (sweet potato & Qing population); FAO 'The potato's travel through ages'. (Grokipedia checked first per source-priority; grokipedia.com/page/Columbian_exchange returned 403 to automated fetch, so corroborated on Wikipedia + academic food-history sources.)
framing_note: Voice: scene-led breadth, one crop-and-direction per rung; never 'What was the Columbian Exchange?'. Accuracy rail: keep directions exact (potato/tomato/chili/chocolate/maize = Americas OUT; wheat/cattle/pigs/sugar/coffee = Old World IN) and no anachronism. Every answer names a FOOD or food animal, never a treaty/date. Payoff rung = T4/T5 (the crops fed population booms in China and Africa).

name: The potato remade the Old World
scope: How a humble Andean tuber became the engine food of Europe. T1: the potato is not European — it comes from the high Andes of South America (Peru/Bolivia) (answer: the potato's homeland = the Andes / South America). T2: an acre of potatoes yields far more food than an acre of grain and grows safely underground — those cheap, dense calories powered Europe's population boom (answer: what made the potato spread = it produced far more calories per field than wheat/rye). T3: the potato is a nightshade — the tuber is food, but green skin and sprouts build a natural toxin, which is why you cut green spots away (answer: why you don't eat green or sprouted potatoes = they form a natural poison). T4: the Andes invented freeze-drying centuries before freezers — stomping potatoes and leaving them out through freezing nights and sunny days makes chuno, storable for years (answer: the ancient Andean freeze-dried potato = chuno). T5: France dismissed the potato as pig food until Antoine Parmentier staged fancy banquets and a for-show guarded field to make it fashionable — a PR campaign for a vegetable (answer: how the potato won over France = a marketing stunt / Parmentier's promotion). Dinner-test: T4 (the Andes freeze-dried potatoes 500 years before the freezer).
source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potato; FAO 'The potato's travel through ages and continents'; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antoine-Augustin_Parmentier; hungyichen.com (potato & Old World demography). (Grokipedia checked first; page 403 to automated fetch, corroborated on Wikipedia/FAO.)
framing_note: Voice: the tuber is the anchor of every rung. Accuracy rail: potato = Andean (Peru/Bolivia), NOT Irish or European; solanine is in green/sprouted parts, the tuber itself is safe (say it kid-plainly). Keep all four choices live — don't leak chuno or Parmentier in the stem. Payoff rung = T4 (chuno, ancient freeze-drying).

name: The Irish Potato Famine
scope: One mold plus one clone crop plus export policy equals catastrophe — food-anchored drama. T2: by the 1840s Ireland's poor lived almost entirely on the potato, a single crop as nearly the whole diet (answer: what Ireland's poor mostly ate = potatoes, almost only). T3: a water mold, potato blight, rotted the crop black in the fields starting 1845 — not drought, not insects (answer: what destroyed the crop = a blight/mold). T4: Ireland grew mostly ONE variety, the 'Lumper,' grown from cuttings so every plant was a near-clone with no genetic defense — the blight tore through all of them at once (answer: why the whole crop failed together = the plants were near-identical clones / a monoculture). T5: as a million died and a million fled, Ireland kept shipping grain and cattle to Britain under the era's landlord and free-market policy — the land produced food even while its people starved (answer: the bitter fact about food during the famine = it kept being exported from Ireland). Dinner-test: T4 (the clone-monoculture science of why it was total).
source: britannica.com/event/Great-Famine-Irish-history; history.com/articles/irish-potato-famine; evolution.berkeley.edu (Monoculture and the Irish Potato Famine); history.com 'After 168 Years, Potato Famine Mystery Solved'. (Grokipedia checked first; corroborated on Britannica + Berkeley evolution site.)
framing_note: Voice: food-anchored history where the FOOD (blight, the Lumper clone, exports) is the anchor, never food-aid geopolitics. Keep the human toll matter-of-fact for a kid, no gore, no polemic. Accuracy rail: state the export fact plainly and attribute policy to the era's landlords/free-market rules — report the FACT, pass NO verdict on blame (a genuinely contested historiography). Payoff rung = T4 (clone monoculture). vision NOT mandated: the answers are food facts, not the bank's stance.

name: The tomato's slow road to Italy
scope: How a Mexican fruit feared as poison became the soul of Italian food. T1: the tomato is not originally Italian — it came from Mexico/the Americas, carried back by the Spanish (answer: the tomato's homeland = Mexico / the Americas). T2: its very name comes from the Aztec (Nahuatl) word 'tomatl' (answer: the language the word 'tomato' comes from = the Aztec/Nahuatl tongue). T3: Europeans feared it for nearly 200 years — it's a nightshade, and its acidic juice leached lead out of the fancy pewter plates of the rich, actually poisoning them, so it earned a 'poison apple' name (answer: why wealthy Europeans got sick from tomatoes = acid pulling lead from pewter plates, not the fruit itself). T4: the first known Italian tomato recipe appears in Naples in 1692 (Antonio Latini) — and he labeled it 'alla spagnuola,' Spanish-style, not Italian (answer: what the first Italian tomato sauce was called = Spanish-style). T5: tomato-on-pasta as a 'classic' is only about 200 years old — for most of Italian history there was no tomato in the kitchen at all (answer: how old red-sauce pasta really is = roughly 200 years / 1800s, not ancient). Dinner-test: T3 (the lead-plate poisoning myth-with-a-real-cause).
source: gardeninsider.org tomato history; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tomato; multiple on Antonio Latini's 1692 'Salsa di pomodoro alla spagnuola' (Lo Scalco alla Moderna, Naples). (Grokipedia checked first; corroborated on Wikipedia + food-history sources.)
framing_note: Voice: scene-led, the fruit is the anchor. Hard accuracy rail: NO tomato in Italy before ~1540s and no 'ancient Italian' tomato dishes (the anti-anachronism spine of this sub-strand). Attribute name to Nahuatl, first recipe to Latini 1692. Payoff rung = T3 (acid + pewter, the real reason behind the poison reputation).

name: The chili conquers Asia
scope: The 'pepper' that isn't pepper, and how it took over Asian cooking only after 1492. T1: chili peppers are from the Americas (Mexico/South America) — before Columbus there was NO chili in India, Thailand, or China (answer: where chilis came from = the Americas). T2: it was Portuguese traders who carried chili to India (Goa) and around Asia in the 1500s (answer: who brought chili to Asia = Portuguese traders). T3: before chili, Asian cooks got their heat from black pepper, long pepper, ginger, and — in China — the numbing Sichuan pepper (answer: what made Asian food hot before chili = black pepper/ginger/Sichuan pepper). T4: the burn isn't taste and isn't real damage — capsaicin fools the very nerve sensor that detects actual heat, so your mouth feels a fire that isn't there (answer: why chili feels hot = it tricks a heat-sensing nerve, with no real burning). T5: milk beats water for killing chili burn because the heat compound is oily, and milk's fat and proteins wash it away while water only spreads it around (answer: what actually cools a chili burn = milk/dairy, because the heat compound is oil-based). Dinner-test: T5 (a fact a kid can USE at the dinner table tonight).
source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chili_pepper; legalnomads.com 'A Brief History of Chili Peppers'; archive-yaleglobal.yale.edu 'Chili: Small Fruit Sets Global Palettes on Fire'. (Grokipedia checked first; corroborated on Wikipedia + YaleGlobal.)
framing_note: Voice: the chili is the anchor; mechanism rungs stay concept-level. Hard accuracy rail: NO chili in Asia pre-Columbus (Portuguese carried it, 1500s) — a flagship anti-anachronism. Keep capsaicin as 'the heat-sensing nerve,' never the Latin receptor name (banned lab jargon). Payoff rung = T5 (milk vs water — usable knowledge).

name: Chocolate: from bitter Aztec drink to sweet bar
scope: Cacao's journey from sacred Mesoamerican drink to the modern candy bar. T1: chocolate began as a DRINK, not a bar — the Maya and Aztec drank it (answer: the original form of chocolate = a drink). T2: that drink, xocolatl, was BITTER and often spiced with chili, with no sugar at all (answer: what Aztec chocolate tasted like = bitter/spiced, not sweet). T3: cacao beans were so prized they served as MONEY — you could literally buy goods with a handful of beans (answer: what cacao beans were used as = currency/money). T4: Europeans transformed it by adding SUGAR (plus vanilla and cinnamon), turning the bitter ritual drink into a sweet treat (answer: what Europeans added to chocolate = sugar). T5: chocolate stayed a drink for roughly 300 years — the solid EATING bar arrived only in 1847 (Fry's), once presses could separate out cocoa butter (answer: the solid chocolate bar you eat was invented in the = 1800s, very recently). Dinner-test: T3 (cacao beans as money — 'money that grew on trees').
source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_chocolate; kew.org 'Food of the gods: a brief history of chocolate'; history.com/articles/history-of-chocolate; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J._S._Fry_%26_Sons (1847 solid bar); Van Houten Dutch-process 1828. (Grokipedia checked first; corroborated on Wikipedia/Kew.)
framing_note: Voice: cacao is the anchor of every rung. Accuracy rail: chocolate was a DRINK for ~300 years; the eating BAR is 19th-century (Fry 1847) — do not imply Aztecs had chocolate bars. Bitter/spiced original, sugar is the European addition. Payoff rung = T3 (beans as currency).

name: Maize goes global, and the pellagra trap
scope: Why corn fed the Americas safely but sickened the Old World. T2: maize (corn) is a Mesoamerican crop — Native Americans bred it from a wild grass, and it spread worldwide after 1492 (answer: where corn comes from = Mexico / Mesoamerica). T3: Mesoamericans soaked their corn in an alkaline lime-or-ash solution before cooking (nixtamalization) — that's how you get the masa dough for tortillas (answer: the ancient corn-prep step = soaking it in lime/ash). T4: that lime step unlocks a vitamin (niacin, B3) that the body simply can't absorb from plain untreated corn — Native cooks got it; Europeans copied the crop but skipped the step (answer: what the lime treatment actually does = frees up a vitamin the body needs). T5: Europe and the American South ate corn as polenta and grits WITHOUT the lime step and suffered pellagra, a deadly deficiency disease — proof the missing piece was the cooking wisdom, not the crop (answer: why corn-eaters fell ill = they skipped the lime-soaking step, not the corn's fault). Dinner-test: T5 (it wasn't the corn, it was the lost technique).
source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nixtamalization; southernfoodways.org 'Malnourished: Cultural ignorance paved the way for pellagra'; link.springer.com B3/niacin nixtamalization study. (Grokipedia checked first; corroborated on Wikipedia + Southern Foodways + Springer.)
framing_note: Voice: corn and the tortilla/polenta are the anchor. Accuracy rail: corn = Mesoamerican; nixtamalization uses alkaline lime/ash; teach the CONCEPT (a freed vitamin) — do NOT test 'niacin' spelling or any microbe/Latin/percentage (banned minutiae; the vitamin name is context only). Payoff rung = T5 (the technique, not the crop, was missing).

name: Sugar: the sweet that crossed the ocean
scope: How sugar went from Old World luxury to New World plantation crop. T2: before cheap sugar, Europeans sweetened food with HONEY — sugar was a rare luxury sold in pinches like a spice at the apothecary (answer: what Europe sweetened with before cheap sugar = honey). T3: sugarcane is an OLD World plant (from New Guinea/Asia) — it traveled the reverse direction, carried TO the Americas by Columbus on his second voyage in 1493 (answer: which way sugar traveled in the Exchange = Old World to the Americas). T4: the Caribbean and Brazil became the world's sugar engine, and suddenly-cheap sugar reshaped European diets — tea, coffee, jam, and candy all leaned on it (answer: where the world's sugar came to be grown = Caribbean/Brazil plantations). T5: turning cane into sugar is a brutal race against time — cut cane must be crushed and boiled within about a day or it spoils, which is why sugar-making ran like a round-the-clock factory (answer: why sugar-making was so relentless = cut cane spoils within roughly a day). Dinner-test: T5 (the 24-hour spoilage race behind the factory-like mills).
source: worldhistory.org 'Sugar & the Rise of the Plantation System'; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_sugar; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbian_exchange (Columbus 1493 cane). (Grokipedia checked first; corroborated on World History Encyclopedia + Wikipedia.)
framing_note: Voice: sugar/cane is the anchor; a prep-frame ('crush and boil the cane') fits cooking. Accuracy rail: cane = Old World (New Guinea/Asia) carried WEST by Columbus 1493 — a reverse-direction rung; keep it distinct from the New-World crops. Sugar's link to slavery is real: state the plantation-labor fact once, plainly and kid-appropriately, keep every tested answer on the food/crop/technique, no polemic. Payoff rung = T5 (spoilage-race mechanism).

name: Coffee crosses to the New World
scope: An Old World bean that the Americas came to dominate — a reverse-direction gem. T2: coffee is NOT American — the coffee plant comes from Ethiopia and Arabia (Yemen), an Old World crop (answer: where coffee originally comes from = Ethiopia/Arabia). T3: coffee crossed the ocean the OTHER way — Europeans planted it in the Americas in the 1700s (answer: when/how coffee reached the Americas = the 1700s, planted by Europeans). T4: today Brazil grows about a THIRD of all the world's coffee — an African-Arabian bean that found its biggest home in the New World (answer: the country that became the world's coffee giant = Brazil). Dinner-test: T4 (Brazil #1 from a bean that isn't even American).
source: britannica.com/topic/history-of-coffee; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_coffee (Brazil via Francisco de Melo Palheta, early 1700s). (Grokipedia checked first; corroborated on Britannica + Wikipedia.)
framing_note: Voice: the bean is the anchor; this ladder's whole point is the REVERSE direction (Old World -> Americas) as a foil to the potato/tomato/chili ladders. Accuracy rail: coffee = Ethiopian/Arabian, NOT American; it arrived in the Americas in the 1700s. Payoff rung = T4 (Brazil grows ~1/3 of world coffee).

name: The turkey's transatlantic name mix-up
scope: The dinner bird everyone assumed came from somewhere it didn't. T1: the turkey is a NORTH AMERICAN bird, native to the Americas — not Europe, not Asia (answer: where turkeys come from = North America/Mexico). T2: the English named it 'turkey' by mistake — they muddled it with an African guinea fowl that reached Europe through the country Turkey (answer: why it's called a turkey = it was confused with a bird traded via Turkey). T3: other languages made the same blunder in the other direction — the French call it 'dinde,' meaning 'from India,' because early explorers thought the Americas were the Indies (answer: what the French word 'dinde' literally means = 'from India'). Dinner-test: T3 (the 'from India' name — a whole language got the bird's origin wrong).
source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turkey_(bird); nationalgeographic.com 'Fowl Play? The Twisted Linguistics of Turkey'. (Grokipedia checked first; corroborated on Wikipedia + National Geographic.)
framing_note: Voice: light, fun food fact; the bird is the anchor. Accuracy rail: turkey = North American, and the naming confusion runs through the guinea fowl / Ottoman Turkey (English) and 'd'Inde' = India (French) — get both directions right. Payoff rung = T3 (the 'dinde'/India name).

name: The spice hunt that launched 1492
scope: Columbus sailed for FLAVOR and mislabeled what he found. T2: Columbus's whole voyage was a hunt for a sea route to the spice lands — pepper, cloves, nutmeg, and cinnamon were worth fortunes in Europe (answer: what Columbus was really sailing after = spices / a spice route). T3: he never found true black pepper, but he found the chili and called it 'pepper' (pimiento) anyway — which is why we still say 'chili pepper' and 'bell pepper' for a fruit unrelated to real pepper (answer: why chilis are called 'peppers' = Columbus mislabeled them while hunting pepper). T4: another New World find, allspice, earned its name because a single berry TASTES like a blend of cloves, cinnamon, and nutmeg — one spice mimicking three (answer: why allspice is called that = it tastes like several Old World spices at once). T5: black pepper was once so precious it was counted out peppercorn by peppercorn and even used to pay rents and ransoms — a spice worth its weight in silver (answer: what pepper was valuable enough to be used as = money / to pay rent). Dinner-test: T3 (chili-called-'pepper' — a naming mistake a kid repeats every day).
source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chili_pepper (Columbus's 'pepper' naming); en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Allspice (named for clove/cinnamon/nutmeg aroma; native to the Greater Antilles); en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peppercorn_(legal). (Grokipedia checked first; corroborated on Wikipedia.)
framing_note: Voice: spices are the anchor — this is the WHY behind the whole Exchange (the voyage was a food-flavor hunt). Accuracy rail: Columbus mislabeled capsicum as 'pepper'; allspice is a single New World berry (Jamaica), not a manufactured blend — label the naming correctly. Payoff rung = T3 (the chili/'pepper' misnomer).
